title: Introduction to Data Visualization
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of introduction to data visualization and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply purpose of data visualization in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Introduction to Data Visualization is part of Data Visualization and Graphics. Start with purpose of data visualization and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: A useful visualization encodes the question honestly with readable scales, descriptive labels and a clear account of uncertainty or limits.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: A useful visualization encodes the question honestly with readable scales, descriptive labels and a clear account of uncertainty or limits. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Choose a chart for the variables, label axes and units, and state what the plot cannot establish. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Introduction to Data Visualization
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 117: Introduction to Data Visualization
plot(c(7, 8, 9), c(2, 5, 4), type = "b", xlab = "Observation", ylab = "Measure")

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For introduction to data visualization, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
